cards.example: Gabriella is gregarious and *garrulous;* she loves to hang out with the gang and gab.

cards.definition: unskillful; awkward; maladroit
cards.example: Smadar had a poor sense of comic timing, and her *gauche* attempts to mock her left-handed friends soon left her with none.
cards.notes:
= socially awkward
Remember *dextrous*? Well, *gauche* is pretty much the exact opposite. It is the French word for left—the connection is that left-handed people were once thought to be clumsy (this was clearly before the invention of left-handed scissors) and perverse, even evil. These days, *gauche* tends to describe social, rather than physical, ineptness.

cards.definition: a type or category, especially of art or writing
cards.example: Daoyen displayed a great talent for a particular *genre:* the bawdy limerick.
cards.notes:
= type of art
The novel is one literary *genre*. Poetry is another.

cards.definition: refined; polite; aristocratic; affecting refinement
cards.example: The ladies at the ball were too *genteel* to accept our invitation to the wrestling match.
cards.notes: A person who is *genteel* has *gentility*.

cards.definition: to make gestures, especially when speaking or in place of speaking
cards.example:
Massimo *gesticulated* wildly on the other side of the theater in an attempt to get our attention.
The after-dinner speaker *gesticulated* in such a strange way that the audience paid more attention to his hands than to his words.
cards.notes: A person who *gesticulates* makes *gesticulations*.

cards.definition: surplus; an overabundance
cards.example:
The international oil shortage turned into an international oil *glut* with surprising speed.
We had a *glut* of contributions but a dearth, or scarcity, of volunteers; it seemed that people would rather give their money than their time.

cards.definition: pompous; using a lot of big, fancy words in an attempt to sound impressive
cards.example:
The governor’s speech was *grandiloquent* rather than eloquent; there were some six-dollar words and some impressive phrases, but he really had nothing to say.
The new minister’s *grandiloquence* got him in trouble with deacons, who wanted him to be more restrained in his sermons.

cards.definition: absurdly exaggerated
cards.example:
The scientist’s *grandiose* plan was to build a huge shopping center on the surface of the moon.
Their house was genuinely impressive, although there were a few *grandiose* touches: a fireplace the size of a garage, a kitchen with four ovens, and a computerized media center in every room.
cards.notes: To be *grandiose* is to be characterized by *grandiosity* (gran dee AHS uh tee).

cards.definition: given freely (said of something bad); unjustified; unprovoked; uncalled for
cards.example:
The scathing review of the movie contained several *gratuitous* remarks about the sex life of the director.
Their attack against us was *gratuitous;* we had never done anything to offend them.
cards.notes: *Gratuitous* is often misunderstood because it is confused with *gratuity*. A *gratuity* is a tip, like the one you leave in a restaurant. A *gratuity* is a nice thing. *Gratuitous*, however, is not nice. Don’t confuse these words.

cards.definition: seriousness
cards.example:
The anchorman’s nervous giggling was entirely inappropriate, given the *gravity* of the situation.
No one realized the *gravity* of Myron’s drug addiction until it was much too late to help him.
cards.notes:
*Gravity* is the force that makes apples fall down instead of up, and the word also carries a different sort of weightiness.
At the heart of the word *gravity* is the word *grave*, which means serious.

cards.definition: sociable; enjoying the company of others
cards.example:
Dirk was too *gregarious* to enjoy the fifteen years he spent in solitary confinement.
Kyle wasn’t very *gregarious;* she went to the party, but she spent most of her time hiding in a closet.
cards.notes: In biology, *gregarious* is used to describe animals that live in groups. Bees, which live together in large colonies, are said to be *gregarious* insects.

cards.definition: cunning; duplicity; artfulness
cards.example:
José used *guile*, not intelligence, to win the spelling bee; he cheated.
Stuart was shocked by the *guile* of the automobile mechanic, who had poked a hole in his radiator and then told him that it had sprung a leak.
Clarence found Mary’s beauty so *beguiling* that he did anything she asked of him.
cards.notes:
To be *guileless* is to be innocent or naive. *Guileless* and *artless* are synonyms.
The word *beguile* also means to deceive, but in a charming and not always bad way.

cards.definition: overused; trite; stale
cards.example:
Michael’s book was full of clichés and *hackneyed* phrases.
The intelligent design issue had been discussed so much as to become *hackneyed*.
cards.notes:
= overused trite
“As cold as ice” is a *hackneyed* expression.

cards.definition: unlucky
cards.example:
Joe’s *hapless* search for fun led him from one disappointment to another.
Alex led a *hapless* existence that made all his friends’ lives seem fortunate by comparison.

cards.definition: a forerunner; a signal of
cards.example: A cloud of bad breath and body odor, which preceded him by several yards everywhere he went, was Harold’s *harbinger*.
cards.notes: Warm weather is the *harbinger* of spring.

cards.definition: the pursuit of pleasure as a way of life
cards.example: Yoshi’s life of *hedonism* came to an end when his lottery winnings ran out; his massaging armchair and wide-screen TV were repossessed, he had to eat macaroni and cheese instead of champagne and lobster, and he could no longer pay to have models fan him with palm fronds and feed him grapes.
cards.notes:
= lifelong pursuit of pleasure
A *hedonist* practices *hedonism* twenty-four hours a day.

cards.definition: leadership, especially of one nation over another
cards.example:
America once held an unchallenged nuclear *hegemony*.
Japan and Germany vie for *hegemony* in the foreign-car market.

cards.definition: any belief that is strongly opposed to established beliefs
cards.notes:
= strongly contrary belief
Galileo was tried for the *heresy* of suggesting that the sun did not revolve around Earth. He was almost convicted of being a *heretic* (HER uh tik), but he recanted his *heretical* (huh RET i kul) view.

cards.definition: impervious to external influence; airtight
cards.example:
The president led a *hermetic* existence in the White House, as his advisers attempted to seal him off from the outside world.
The old men felt vulnerable and unwanted outside the *hermetic* security of their club.
The poisonous substance was sealed *hermetically* inside a glass cylinder.

cards.definition: golden age; prime
cards.example:
In his *heyday*, Vernon was a world-class athlete; today he’s just Vernon.
The *heyday* of the British Navy ended a long, long time ago.

cards.definition: a break or interruption, often from work
cards.example: Spencer looked forward to spring break as a welcome *hiatus* from the rigors of campus parties.

cards.definition: an organization based on rank or degree; pecking order
cards.example:
Kendra was very low in the State Department *hierarchy*. In fact, her phone number wasn’t even listed in the State Department directory.
There appeared to be no *hierarchy* in the newly discovered tribe; there were no leaders and, for that matter, no followers.
cards.notes: The adjective is *hierarchical* (hye uh RAHRK i kul).

cards.definition: overly dramatic; theatrical
cards.example:
Adele’s *histrionic* request for a raise embarrassed everyone in the office. She gesticulated wildly, jumped up and down, pulled out handfuls of hair, threw herself to the ground, and groaned in agony.
The chairman’s *histrionic* presentation persuaded no one.
The young actor’s *histrionics* made everyone in the audience squirm.
cards.notes: *Histrionic* behavior is referred to as *histrionics*.

cards.definition: a sermon
cards.example: The football coach often began practice with a lengthy *homily* on the virtues of clean living.

cards.definition: uniform; made entirely of one thing
cards.example:
The kindergarten class was extremely *homogeneous:* All the children had blond hair, blue eyes, red shoes, and the same last name.
On Halloween the children amassed a *heterogeneous* collection of candy, chewing gum, popcorn, and cookies.
cards.notes:
*Homogenized* (huh MAHJ uh nyzed) milk is milk in which the cream, which usually floats on top, has been permanently mixed with the rest of the milk. (Skim milk is milk from which the layer of cream has been skimmed off.) When milk is *homogenized*, it becomes a *homogeneous* substance—that is, it’s the same throughout, or uniform.
To be *heterogeneous* (het ur uh JEE nee us) is to be mixed or varied.
The nouns are *homogeneity* (hoh muh juh NEE uh tee) and *heterogeneity* (het uh roh juh NEE uh tee), respectively.

cards.definition: thrifty management of resources; livestock farming
cards.example: Everyone *husbanded* oil and electricity during the energy crisis of the 1970s.
cards.notes: *Husbandry* is the practice of conserving money or resources. To *husband* is to economize.

cards.definition: an exaggeration used as a figure of speech; exaggeration
cards.example:
When Joe said, “I’m so hungry I could eat a horse,” he was using *hyperbole* to convey the extent of his hunger.
The candidate was guilty of *hyperbole;* all the facts in his speech were exaggerated.

cards.definition: uncertain; unproven
cards.example: There were several *hypothetical* explanations for the strange phenomenon, but no one could say for certain what had caused it.
cards.notes: A *hypothetical* explanation is a *hypothesis* (hye PAHTH uh sis), the plural of which is *hypotheses* (hye PAHTH uh seez).

cards.definition: one who attacks popular beliefs or institutions
cards.example:
The popular columnist was an inveterate *iconoclast*, avidly attacking public figures no matter what their party affiliations.
To study and go to class is to be an *iconoclast* on that particular campus, which has a reputation for being the biggest party school in the country.
Herbert’s *iconoclastic* (eye kahn uh KLAS tik) views were not popular with the older members of the board.
cards.notes:
= attacker of popular beliefs
*Iconoclast* comes from Greek words meaning image breaker. The original *iconoclasts* were opponents of the use of *icons*, or sacred images, in certain Christian churches. Today the word is used to refer to someone who attacks popular figures and ideas—a person to whom “nothing is sacred.”

cards.definition: a system of social or political ideas
cards.example:
The candidate never managed to communicate his *ideology* to the voters, so few people were able to grasp what he stood for.
The senator’s tax proposal had more to do with *ideology* than with common sense; his plan, though consistent with his principles, was clearly impractical.
cards.notes:
= system of social ideas
Conservatism and liberalism are competing *ideologies*.
A dogmatic person attached to an *ideology* is an *ideologue* (EYE dee uh lawg). An *ideologue* is doctrinaire.
*Ideology* is sometimes pronounced “ID ee ahl uh jee.”

cards.pron: id ee oh SINK ruh see
cards.definition: a peculiarity; an eccentricity
cards.example:
Eating green beans drenched in ketchup for breakfast was one of Jordana’s *idiosyncrasies*.
The doctor’s interest was aroused by an *idiosyncrasy* in Bill’s skull: There seemed to be a coin slot in the back of his head.
Tara’s driving was somewhat *idiosyncratic;* she sometimes seemed to prefer the sidewalk to the street.
cards.notes: A person who has an *idiosyncrasy* is said to be *idiosyncratic* (id ee oh sin KRAT ik).

cards.definition: charming in a rustic way; naturally peaceful
cards.example:
They built their house on an *idyllic* spot. There was a babbling brook in back and an unbroken view of wooded hills in front.
Our vacation in the country was *idyllic;* we went for long walks down winding dirt roads and didn’t watch television all week.
cards.notes: An *idyllic* time or place could also be called an *idyll* (EYE dul).

cards.definition: deep disgrace
cards.example:
After the big scandal, the formerly high-flying investment banker fell into a life of shame and *ignominy*.
The *ignominy* of losing the spelling bee was too much for Arnold, who decided to give up spelling altogether.
Lola’s plagiarizing of Nabokov’s work was an *ignominious* act that got her suspended from school for two days.
cards.notes: Something that is deeply disgraceful is *ignominious* (ig nuh MIN ee us).

cards.definition: illegal; not permitted
cards.example: The police interviewed hundreds of witnesses, trying to *elicit* clues that might help them stop an *illicit* business.
cards.notes:
Criminals engage in *illicit* activities.
Don’t confuse this word with *elicit*, listed previously.

cards.definition: to move permanently to a new country
cards.example: Edwin *immigrated* to Canada, thinking the move would give his two-year-old daughter a better shot at attending the University of Toronto preschool.
cards.notes:
It’s easy to confuse this word with *emigrate*. To avoid this, just remember that *emigrate* means *e*xit, and *immigrate* means come *in*.
The noun form of the word is *immigration*.

cards.definition: just about to happen
cards.example:
The pink glow in the east made it clear that sunrise was *imminent*.
Patrice had a strange feeling that disaster was *imminent*, then the jumbo jet crashed into her garage.
cards.notes: Don’t confuse this word with *eminent*, listed previously.

cards.definition: unchangeable
cards.example:
Jerry’s mother had only one *immutable* rule: no dancing on the dinner table.
The statue of the former principal looked down on the students with an *immutable* scowl.
The *mutable* shoreline shifted continually as the tides moved sand first in one direction and then in another.
Sonrisa’s moods were *mutable;* one minute she was kind and gentle; the next minute she was screaming with anger.
cards.notes:
Something that is changeable is said to be *mutable*.
Both *immutable* and *mutable* are based on a Latin root meaning change. So are *mutation* and *mutant*.

cards.definition: fair; not favoring one side or the other; unbiased
cards.example:
Jurors are supposed to be *impartial* rather than *partial;* they aren’t supposed to make up their minds until they’ve heard all the evidence.
Beverly tried to be an *impartial* judge at the beauty contest, but in the end she couldn’t help selecting her own daughter to be the new Honeybee Queen.
cards.notes: The noun is *impartiality* (im pahr shee AL uh tee).

cards.definition: flawless; entirely without sin
cards.example:
The children’s behavior was *impeccable;* they didn’t pour dye into the swimming pool.
Hal’s clothes were always *impeccable;* even the wrinkles were perfectly creased.
cards.notes: By the way, *peccable* means liable to sin. And while we’re at it, a *peccadillo* is a minor sin.

cards.definition: like an emperor or an empire
cards.example:
The palace was decorated with *imperial* splendor.
George’s *imperial* manner was inappropriate since he was nothing more exalted than the local dogcatcher.
The director’s *imperious* style rubbed everyone the wrong way; he always seemed to be giving orders, and he never listened to what anyone said.
cards.notes:
*Imperial, emperor*, and *empire* are all derived from the same root. England’s *imperial* days are over, now that the British Empire has broken apart.
A similar word is *imperious* (im PEER ee us), which means bossy and, usually, arrogant.

cards.definition: not allowing anything to pass through; impenetrable
cards.example:
A raincoat, if it is any good, is *impervious* to water. It is made of an *impervious* material.
David was *impervious* to criticism—he did what he wanted to do no matter what anyone said.

cards.definition: impulsive; extremely impatient
cards.example:
*Impetuous* Dick always seemed to be running off to buy a new car, even if he had just bought one the month before.
Samantha was so *impetuous* that she never took more than a few seconds to make up her mind.

cards.definition: to carry out
cards.example:
Leo developed a plan for shortening the grass in his yard, but he was unable to *implement* it because he didn’t have a lawn mower.
The government was better at creating new laws than it was at *implementing* them.

cards.definition: powerless; helpless; unable to perform
cards.example:
Joe and Olga made a few *impotent* efforts to turn aside the steamroller, but it squished their vegetable garden anyway.
We felt *impotent* in the face of their overpowering opposition to our plan.
cards.notes:
*Impotent* means not *potent*—not powerful.
*Omnipotent* (ahm NIP uh tunt) means all powerful. After winning a dozen games in a row, the football team began to feel *omnipotent*.

cards.definition: to attack, especially to attack the truth or integrity of something
cards.example:
The critic *impugned* the originality of Jacob’s novel, claiming that long stretches of it had been lifted from the work of someone else.
Fred said I was *impugning* his honesty when I called him a dirty liar, but I told him he had no honesty to *impugn*. This just seemed to make him angrier.
cards.notes: = attack the truth of

cards.definition: silly; senseless
cards.example:
Their plan to make an indoor swimming pool by flooding their basement was *inane*.
Mel made a few *inane* comments about the importance of chewing only on the left side of one’s mouth, and then he passed out beneath the table.
cards.notes: Something that is *inane* is an *inanity* (i NAN i tee).

cards.definition: to begin officially; to induct formally into office
cards.example:
The mayor *inaugurated* the new no-smoking policy and then celebrated by lighting up a big cigar.
The team’s loss *inaugurated* an era of defeat that lasted for several years.
cards.notes: To *inaugurate* a U.S. president is to make him take the oath of office and then give him the keys to the White House.

cards.definition: brilliant; giving off heat or light
cards.example: Jan’s ideas were so *incandescent* that simply being near her made you feel as though you understood the subject for the first time.
cards.notes: An *incandescent* light bulb is one containing a wire or filament that gives off light when it is heated. An *incandescent* person is one who gives off light or energy in a figurative sense.

cards.definition: a chant; the repetition of statements or phrases in a way reminiscent of a chant
cards.example:
Much to our delight, the wizard’s *incantation* eventually caused the small stone to turn into a sleek black BMW.
The students quickly became deaf to the principal’s *incantations* about the importance of school spirit.

cards.definition: to make very angry
cards.example:
Jeremy was *incensed* when I told him that even though he was stupid and loathsome, he would always be my best friend.
My comment about the lovely painting of a tree *incensed* the artist, who said it was actually a portrait of his mother.

cards.definition: unceasing
cards.example:
I will go deaf and lose my mind if your children don’t stop the *incessant* bickering.
The noise from the city street was *incessant;* there always seemed to be a fire engine or a police car screaming by.
cards.notes: A *cessation* is a ceasing.

cards.definition: beginning; emerging
cards.example:
Sitting in class, Henrietta detected an *incipient* tingle of boredom that told her she would soon be asleep.
Support for the plan was *incipient*, and the planners hoped it would soon grow and spread.
cards.notes: The *inception* of something is its start or formal beginning.

cards.definition: cutting right to the heart of the matter
cards.example:
After hours of debate, Louis offered a few *incisive* comments that made it immediately clear to everyone how dumb the original idea had been.
Lloyd’s essays were always *incisive;* he never wasted any words, and his reasoning was sharp and persuasive.
cards.notes: When a surgeon cuts into you, he or she makes an *incision*. To be *incisive* is to be as sharp as a scalpel in a figurative sense.

cards.definition: not harmonious; not consistent; not appropriate; not fitting in
cards.example:
The ultramodern kitchen seemed *incongruous* in the restored eighteenth-century farmhouse. It was an *incongruity* (in kun GROO uh tee).
Bill’s membership in the motorcycle gang was *incongruous* with his mild personality and his career as a management consultant.

cards.definition: incapable of being reformed
cards.example:
The convict was an *incorrigible* criminal; as soon as he got out of prison, he said, he was going to rob another doughnut store.
Bill is *incorrigible*—he eats three bags of potato chips every day even though he knows that eating two would be better for him.
The ever-cheerful Annie is an *incorrigible* optimist.
cards.notes: Think of *incorrigible* as incorrectable. The word *corrigible* is rarely seen or used these days.

cards.definition: an increase; one in a series of increases
cards.example:
Bernard received a small *increment* in his salary each year, even though he did less and less work with every day that passed.
This year’s fund-raising total represented an *increment* of 1 percent over last year’s. This year’s total represented an *incremental* change from last year’s.
Doug built up his savings account *incrementally*, one dollar at a time.

cards.definition: not caring one way or the other; apathetic; mediocre
cards.example:
Pedro was *indifferent* about politics; he didn’t care who was elected to office so long as no one passed a law against Monday Night Football.
Henry’s *indifference* was extremely annoying to Melissa, who loved to argue but found it difficult to do so with people who had no opinions.
We planted a big garden but the results were *indifferent;* only about half of the flowers came up.
The painter did an *indifferent* job, but it was good enough for Susan, who was *indifferent* about painting.
cards.notes: = not caring; mediocre

cards.definition: native; originating in that area
cards.example:
Fast-food restaurants are *indigenous* to America, where they were invented.
The grocer said the corn had been locally grown, but it didn’t appear to be *indigenous*.
The botanist said that the small cactus was *indigenous* but that the large one had been introduced to the region by Spanish explorers.

cards.definition: poor
cards.example:
The *indigent* family had little to eat, nothing to spend, and virtually nothing to wear.
Rusty had once been a lawyer but now was *indigent;* he spent most of his time sleeping on a bench in the park.
cards.notes: Don’t confuse this word with *indigenous*, listed earlier.

cards.definition: angry, especially as a result of something unjust or unworthy; insulted
cards.example:
Ted became *indignant* when the policewoman accused him of stealing the nuclear weapon.
Isabel was *indignant* when we told her all the nasty things that Blake had said about her over the public address system.

cards.definition: lazy
cards.example:
The *indolent* teenagers slept late, moped around, and never looked for summer jobs.
Inheriting a lot of money enabled Rodney to do what he loved most: pursue a life of *indolence*.

cards.definition: lenient; yielding to desire
cards.example:
The nice mom was *indulgent* of her children, letting them have all the candy, cookies, and ice cream that they wanted, even for breakfast.
Our *indulgent* teacher never punished us for not turning in our homework. She didn’t want us to turn into ascetic grinds.
cards.notes: Someone who is *self-indulgent* yields to his or her every desire.

cards.definition: incapable of being expressed or described
cards.example: The simple beauty of nature is often so *ineffable* that it brings tears to our eyes.
cards.notes:
= inexpressible
The word *effable*—expressible—is rarely used.

cards.definition: clumsy; incompetent; gauche
cards.example:
Joshua is an *inept* dancer; he is as likely to stomp on his partner’s foot as he is to step on it.
Julia’s *inept* attempt at humor drew only groans from the audience.
The woodworking class’s *ineptitude* was broad and deep; there was little that they were able to do and nothing that they were able to do well.
cards.notes:
To be *inept* is to be characterized by *ineptitude*, which is the opposite of aptitude.
The opposite of *inept* is *adept* (uh DEPT). *Adept* and *adroit* are synonyms.

cards.definition: inactive; sluggish; not reacting chemically
cards.example:
The baseball team seemed strangely *inert;* it was as though they had lost the will to play.
Having colds made the children *inert* and reluctant to get out of bed.
Helium is an *inert* gas: It doesn’t burn, it doesn’t explode, and it doesn’t kill you if you inhale it.
cards.notes:
To be *inert* is to be characterized by *inertia*. As it is most commonly used, *inertia* means lack of get-up-and-go, or an inability or unwillingness to move.
In physics, *inertia* refers to an object’s tendency to continue doing what it’s doing (either moving or staying still) unless it’s acted on by something else.

cards.definition: relentless; inevitable; unavoidable
cards.example:
The *inexorable* waves pounded the shore, as they have always pounded it and as they always will pound it.
Eliot drove his father’s car slowly but *inexorably* through the grocery store, wrecking aisle after aisle despite the manager’s anguished pleading.
*Inexorable* death finds everyone sooner or later.

cards.definition: shamefully wicked; having an extremely bad reputation; disgraceful
cards.example:
Deep within the prison was the *infamous* torture chamber, where hooded guards tickled their prisoners with feathers until they confessed.
The former Nazi lived the rest of his life in *infamy* after the court convicted him of war crimes and atrocities.
President Roosevelt said that the date of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor would “live in *infamy*.”
cards.notes:
Be careful with the pronunciation of this word.
To be *infamous* is to be *famous* for being evil or bad. An *infamous* cheater is one whose cheating is well known.
*Infamy* is the state of being *infamous*.

cards.definition: foolish; foolishly passionate or attracted; made foolish; foolishly in love
cards.example:
I was so *infatuated* with Polly that I drooled and gurgled whenever she was near.
The *infatuated* candidate thought so highly of himself that he had the walls of his house covered with his campaign posters.
My ride in Boris’s racing car *infatuated* me; I knew immediately that I would have to have a racing car, too.
cards.notes: To be *infatuated* is to be *fatuous* or foolish.

cards.definition: to conclude; to deduce
cards.example:
Raizel said she loved the brownies, but I *inferred* from the size of the piece left on her plate that she had actually despised them.
She hadn’t heard the score, but the silence in the locker room led her to *infer* that we had lost.
cards.notes:
*Infer* is often confused with *imply*. To *imply* something is to hint at it, suggest it, or state it indirectly. To *infer* something is to figure out what it is without being told directly.
An *inference* is a deduction or conclusion.

cards.pron: in fin uh TES uh mul
cards.definition: very, very, very small; infinitely small
cards.example:
An *infinitesimal* bug of some kind crawled into Heather’s ear and bit her in a place she couldn’t scratch.
Our chances of winning were *infinitesimal*, but we played our hearts out anyway.
cards.notes: *Infinitesimal* does not mean huge, as some people incorrectly believe.

cards.definition: frank; without deception; simple; artless; charmingly naive
cards.example:
A young child is *ingenuous*. He doesn’t know much about the ways of the world, and certainly not enough to deceive anyone.
An *ingenue* (AHN ji noo) is a somewhat naive young woman, especially a movie actress or character.
The movie producer was being *disingenuous* when he said, “I don’t care about making money on this movie. I just want every man, woman, and child in the country to see it.”
cards.notes: *Disingenuous* means crafty or artful.

cards.definition: part of the essential nature of something; intrinsic
cards.example:
There is an *inherent* strength in steel that cardboard lacks.
The man’s *inherent* fatness, jolliness, and beardedness made it easy for him to play the part of Santa Claus.
cards.notes:
= part of the nature of
Wetness is an *inherent* quality of water. (You could also say that wetness is *inherent* in water.)

cards.definition: a command or order, especially a court order
cards.example:
Wendy’s neighbors got a court *injunction* prohibiting her from playing her radio.
Herbert, lighting up, disobeyed his doctor’s *injunction* to stop smoking.

cards.definition: existing since birth; inborn; inherent
cards.example:
Joseph’s kindness was *innate;* it was part of his natural character.
Bill has an apparently *innate* ability to throw a football. You just can’t teach someone to throw a ball as well as he can.
There’s nothing *innate* about good manners; all children have to be taught to say “Please” and “Thank you.”

cards.definition: harmless; banal
cards.example:
The speaker’s voice was loud but his words were *innocuous;* there was nothing to get excited about.
Meredith took offense at Bruce’s *innocuous* comment about the saltiness of her soup.
cards.notes: *Innocuous* is closely related, in both origin and meaning, to *innocent*.

cards.definition: excessive; unreasonable
cards.example:
The math teacher paid an *inordinate* amount of attention to the grammar rather than algebra.
The limousine was *inordinately* large, even for a limousine; there was room for more than a dozen passengers.
Romeo’s love for Juliet was perhaps a bit *inordinate*, given the outcome of their relationship.

cards.definition: hard or impossible to satisfy; greedy; avaricious
cards.example:
Peter had an *insatiable* appetite for chocolate macadamia ice cream; he could never get enough. Not even a gallon of chocolate macadamia was enough to *sate* (sayt) or *satiate* (SAY shee ayt) his craving.
Peter’s addiction never reached *satiety* (suh TYE uh tee or SAY she uh tee).

cards.definition: treacherous; sneaky
cards.example:
Winter was *insidious;* it crept in under the doors and through cracks in the windows.
Cancer, which can spread rapidly from a small cluster of cells, is an *insidious* disease.

cards.definition: to hint; to creep in
cards.example:
When I told her that I hadn’t done any laundry in a month, Valerie *insinuated* that I was a slob.
He didn’t ask us outright to leave; he merely *insinuated*, through his tone and his gestures, that it was time for us to go.
Jessica *insinuated* her way into the conversation by moving her chair closer and closer to where we were sitting.
cards.notes: To *insinuate* is to make an *insinuation*.

cards.definition: dull; bland; banal
cards.example:
Barney’s jokes were so *insipid* that no one in the room managed to force out so much as a chuckle.
We were bored to death at the party; it was full of *insipid* people making *insipid* conversation.
The thin soup was so *insipid* that all the spices in the world could not have made it interesting.

cards.definition: arrogant; insulting
cards.example:
The ill-mannered four-year-old was so *insolent* that his parents had a hard time finding a babysitter.
The *insolent* sales clerk clearly didn’t like answering customers’ questions.

cards.definition: to provoke; to stir up
cards.example:
The strike was *instigated* by the ambitious union president, who wanted to get his name into the news.
The CIA tried unsuccessfully to *instigate* rebellion in the tiny country by distributing pamphlets that, as it turned out, were printed in the wrong language.

cards.definition: like an island; isolated
cards.example:
The *insular* little community had very little contact with the world around it.
The *insularity* of the little community was so complete that it was impossible to buy a big-city newspaper there.
cards.notes:
The Latin word for island is *insula*. From it we get the words *peninsula* (“almost an island”), *insulate* (*insulation* makes a house an island of heat), and *insular*, among others.
Something that is *insular* has *insularity*.

cards.definition: a rebel; someone who revolts against a government
cards.example: The heavily armed *insurgents* rushed into the presidential palace, but they paused to taste the fresh blueberry pie on the dinner table and were captured by the president’s bodyguards.
cards.notes:
This word can also be an adjective. A rebellion is an *insurgent* activity.
*Insurgency* is another word for rebellion; so is *insurrection*.

cards.definition: essential
cards.example:
A solid offense was an *integral* part of our football team; so was a strong defense.
Dave was *integral* to the organization; it could never have gotten along without him.

cards.definition: to combine two or more things into a whole
cards.example: Marisol’s school offered an *integrated* history and language curriculum so that students learned Roman history and Latin in the same classroom.
cards.notes:
= unite
This word is related to *segregate, aggregate*, and *congregate*, all of which describe joining or separating. It has the same root as *integer*, which means a whole number.
The noun form is *integration*, which often refers to the end of racial segregation.

cards.definition: uncontrollable; stubborn; disobedient
cards.example:
The *intractable* child was a torment to his nursery school teacher.
Lavanya was *intractable* in her opposition to pay increases for the library employees; she swore she would never vote to give them a raise.
The disease was *intractable*. None of the dozens of medicines the doctor tried had the slightest effect on it.
cards.notes: The opposite of *intractable* is *tractable*.

cards.definition: uncompromising; stubborn
cards.example:
Vijay was an *intransigent* hard-liner, and he didn’t care how many people he offended with his views.
The jury was unanimous except for one *intransigent* member, who didn’t believe that anyone should ever be forced to go to jail.
cards.notes: The noun is *intransigence*.

cards.definition: part of the essential nature of something; inherent
cards.example:
Larry’s *intrinsic* boldness was always getting him into trouble.
There was an *intrinsic* problem with Owen’s alibi: It was a lie.
cards.notes: The opposite of *intrinsic* is *extrinsic*.

cards.definition: tending to think about oneself; examining one’s feelings
cards.example:
The *introspective* six-year-old never had much to say to other people but always seemed to be turning something over in her mind.
Randy’s *introspective* examination of his motives led him to conclude that he must have been at fault in the breakup of his marriage.
cards.notes: See *extrovert*, listed previously.

cards.definition: to flood; to cover completely with water; to overwhelm
cards.example:
The tiny island kingdom was *inundated* by the tidal wave. Fortunately, no one died from the deluge.
The mother was *inundated* with telegrams and gifts after she gave birth to octuplets.

cards.definition: insulting or abusive speech
cards.example:
The critic’s searing review was filled with bitterness and *invective*.
Herman wasn’t much of an orator, but he was brilliant at *invective*.
cards.notes: = insulting speech

cards.definition: habitual; firm in habit; deeply rooted
cards.example:
Eric was such an *inveterate* liar on the golf course that when he finally made a hole-in-one, he marked it on his score card as a zero.
Larry’s practice of spitting into the fireplace became *inveterate* despite his wife’s protestations.

cards.definition: easily angered or provoked; irritable
cards.example: The CEO was so *irascible*, his employees were afraid to talk to him for fear he might hurl paperweights at them.
cards.notes: A grouch is *irascible*.

cards.definition: meaning the opposite of what you seem to say; using words to mean something other than what they seem to mean
cards.example:
Eddie was being *ironic* when he said he loved Peter like a brother; in truth, he hated him.
Credulous George never realized that the speaker was being *ironic* as he discussed a plan to put a nuclear-missile silo in every backyard in America.
cards.notes:
= meaning other than what’s said
Don’t use the alternate form, *ironical*.

cards.definition: irreversible
cards.example:
My decision not to wear a Tarzan costume and ride on a float in the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is *irrevocable;* there is absolutely nothing you could do or say to make me change my mind.
After his friend pointed out that the tattoo was spelled incorrectly, Tom realized that his decision to get a tattoo was *irrevocable*.
cards.notes:
To *revoke* (ri VOHK) is to take back. Something *irrevocable* cannot be taken back.
Something that can be reversed is *revocable* (REV uh kuh bul).

cards.definition: moving from place to place
cards.example:
The life of a traveling salesman is an *itinerant* one.
The *itinerant* junk dealer passes through our neighborhood every month or so, pulling his wagon of odds and ends.
The international banker’s *itinerant* lifestyle began to seem less glamorous to him after his first child was born.
The tour guide handed each traveler an *itinerary* of the tour bus route so they would know what to expect throughout the day.
cards.notes: A closely related word is *itinerary*, which is the planned route or schedule of a trip.

cards.definition: exercising sound judgment
cards.example:
The judge was far from *judicious;* he told the jury that he thought the defendant looked guilty and said that anyone who would wear a red bow tie into a courtroom deserved to be sent to jail.
The firefighters made *judicious* use of flame-retardant foam on the brush fire before it spread to nearby homes.
The mother of twin boys *judiciously* used an electron microscope and a laser to divide the ice cream into equal parts.
cards.notes: The word *judicial* is obviously closely related, but there is a critically important difference in meaning between it and *judicious*. A judge is *judicial* simply by virtue of being a judge; *judicial* means having to do with judges, judgment, or justice. But a judge is *judicious* only if he or she exercises sound judgment.

cards.definition: to place side by side
cards.example:
Comedy and tragedy were *juxtaposed* in the play, which was alternately funny and sad.
*Juxtaposing* the genuine painting and the counterfeit made it much easier to tell which was which.
cards.notes: The noun is *juxtaposition* (juk stuh puh ZISH un).

cards.definition: having to do with motion; lively; active
cards.notes:
*Kinetic* energy is energy associated with motion. A speeding bullet has a lot of *kinetic* energy.
*Kinetic* art is art with things in it that move. A mobile is an example of *kinetic* art.
A *kinetic* personality is a lively, active, and moving personality.

cards.definition: a maze; something like a maze
cards.example:
Each of the fifty floors in the office building was a *labyrinth* of dark corridors and narrow passageways.
The bill took many months to pass through the *labyrinth* of congressional approval.
Before beginning construction on the new house, the contractor had to weave his way through the *labyrinthine* bureaucracy in order to obtain a building permit.
cards.notes: A *labyrinth* is *labyrinthine* (lab uh RINTH in, lab uh RINTH ine, or lab uh RINTH een) or mazelike.

cards.definition: using few words, especially to the point of seeming rude
cards.example:
The manager’s *laconic* dismissal letter left the fired employees feeling angry and hurt.
When she went backstage, June discovered why the popular rock musician was so *laconic* in public: His voice was high and squeaky.

cards.definition: to mourn
cards.example:
From the balcony of the bullet-pocked hotel, the foreign correspondents could hear hundreds of women and children *lamenting* the fallen soldiers.
As the snowstorm gained in intensity, Stan *lamented* his decision that morning to dress in shorts and a T-shirt.
cards.notes: *Lamentable* (LAM en tuh bul) or (luh MEN tuh bul) means regrettable.

cards.definition: to satirize; to mock; to parody
cards.example:
The irreverent students mercilessly *lampooned* their Latin teacher’s lisp in a skit at the school talent show.
*The Harvard Lampoon*, the nation’s oldest humor magazine, has *lampooned* just about everything there is to *lampoon*.

cards.definition: to become weak, listless, or depressed
cards.example:
The formerly eager and vigorous accountant *languished* in his tedious job at the international conglomerate.
The longer Jill remained unemployed, the more she *languished* and the less likely it became that she would find another job.
The child seemed so *languid* that his father thought he was sick and called the doctor. It turned out that the little boy had simply had an overdose of television.
cards.notes: To *languish* is to be *languid*.

cards.definition: generous giving of gifts (or the gifts themselves); generosity; philanthropy
cards.example: Sam was marginally literate at best. Only the *largess* of his uncle got Sam into the Ivy League school.
cards.notes: *Largess* can also be spelled *largesse*.

cards.definition: present but not visible or apparent; potential
cards.example: At four, Maria was a *latent* shopaholic; she learned to read by browsing the descriptions in clothing catalogs.

cards.definition: to praise; to applaud; to extol; to celebrate
cards.example: The bank manager *lauded* the hero who trapped the escaping robber. The local newspaper published a *laudatory* editorial on this intrepid individual.
cards.notes:
*Laudatory* means praising.
Giving several million dollars to charity is a *laudable* act of philanthropy. *Laudable* means praiseworthy.

cards.definition: something handed down from the past; a bequest
cards.example:
The *legacy* of the corrupt administration was chaos, bankruptcy, and despair.
A shoebox full of baseball cards was the dead man’s only *legacy*.
To be a *legacy* at a college sorority is to be the daughter of a former sorority member.

cards.definition: sluggishness; laziness; drowsiness; indifference
cards.example:
After a busy week of sports, homework, and work, the student relished the *lethargy* of Saturday morning.
The *lethargy* of the staff caused what should have been a quick errand to expand into a full day’s work.
The *lethargic* (luh THAR jik) teenagers took all summer to paint the Hendersons’ garage.
cards.notes: To be filled with *lethargy* is to be *lethargic*.

cards.definition: lightness; frivolity; unseriousness
cards.example:
The speaker’s *levity* was not appreciated by the convention of funeral directors, who felt that a convention of funeral directors was no place to tell jokes.
The judge’s attempt to inject some *levity* into the dreary court proceedings (by setting off a few firecrackers in the jury box) was entirely successful.
cards.notes: To *levitate* something is to make it so light that it floats up into the air. *Levity* comes from the same root and has to do with a different kind of lightness.

cards.definition: a written or published falsehood that injures the reputation of, or defames, someone
cards.example: The executive said that the newspaper had committed *libel* when it called him a stinking, no-good, corrupt, incompetent, overpaid, lying, worthless moron. He claimed that the newspaper had *libeled* him, and that its description of him had been *libelous*. At the trial, the jury disagreed, saying that the newspaper’s description of the executive had been substantially accurate.
cards.notes:
= written injurious falsehood
Don’t confuse this word with *liable*, which has an entirely different meaning.
*Slander* is just like *libel* except that it is spoken instead of written.
To *slander* someone is to say something untrue that injures that person’s reputation.

cards.definition: to try in court; to engage in legal proceedings
cards.example:
His lawyer thought a lawsuit would be fruitless, but the client wanted to *litigate*. He was feeling *litigious* (li TIJ us); that is, he was feeling in a mood to go to court.
When the company was unable to recover its money outside of court, its only option was to *litigate*.
cards.notes: To *litigate* is to engage in *litigation;* a court hearing is an example of *litigation*.

cards.definition: talking a lot or too much
cards.example:
The child was surprisingly *loquacious* for one so small.
Mary is so *loquacious* that Belinda can sometimes put down the telephone receiver and run a load of laundry while Mary is talking.
The English teacher’s *loquacity* in class left little time for any of the students to speak, which was fine with most of them.
cards.notes: A *loquacious* person is one who is characterized by *loquaciousness* or *loquacity* (loh KWAS uh tee).

cards.definition: clear; easy to understand
cards.example:
The professor’s explanation of the theory of relativity was so astonishingly *lucid* that even I could understand it.
Hubert’s remarks were few but *lucid:* He explained the complicated issue with just a handful of well-chosen words.
The extremely old man was *lucid* right up until the moment he died; his body had given out but his mind was still going strong.
cards.notes: To *elucidate* something is to make it clear, to explain it.

cards.definition: exaggeratedly mournful
cards.example:
Harry’s *lugubrious* eulogy at the funeral of his dog eventually made everyone start giggling.
The valedictorian suddenly turned *lugubrious* and began sobbing and tearing her hair at the thought of graduating from high school.
cards.notes: To be mournful is to be sad and sorrowful. To be *lugubrious* is to make a big show of being sad and sorrowful.

cards.definition: giving off light; glowing; bright
cards.example:
The moon was a *luminous* disk in the cloudy nighttime sky.
The snow on the ground appeared eerily *luminous* at night—it seemed to glow.
The dial on my watch is *luminous;* it casts a green glow in the dark.

cards.definition: scheming activity for an evil purpose
cards.example:
The ruthless *machinations* of the mobsters left a trail of blood and bodies.
The *machinations* of the conspirators were aimed at nothing less than the overthrow of the government.
cards.notes:
= scheming evil activity
This word is almost always used in the plural—*machinations*—in which form it means the same thing.
This word is often used imprecisely to mean something like “machinelike activity.” It should not be used in this way.

cards.definition: forgiving; unresentful; noble in spirit; generous
cards.example:
The boxer was *magnanimous* in defeat, telling the sports reporters that his opponent had simply been too talented for him to beat.
Mrs. Jones *magnanimously* offered the little boy a cookie when he came over to confess that he had accidentally broken her window while playing baseball.
The *magnanimity* of the conquering general was much appreciated by the defeated soldiers.
cards.notes: To be *magnanimous* is to have *magnanimity* (mag nuh NIM uh tee).

cards.definition: a rich, powerful, or very successful businessperson
cards.example: John D. Rockefeller was a *magnate* who was never too cheap to give a shoeshine boy a dime for his troubles.
cards.notes: = rich businessperson

cards.definition: a feeling of depression, uneasiness, or queasiness
cards.example: *Malaise* descended on the calculus class when the teacher announced a quiz.

cards.definition: an illegal act, especially by a public official
cards.example: President Ford officially pardoned former president Nixon before the latter could be convicted of any *malfeasance*.

cards.definition: causing harm
cards.example: Lina has had recurring tumors since the operation; we’re just glad that none of them have proved *malignant*.
cards.notes:
= deadly
Many words that start with *mal-* connote evil or harm, just as words that begin with *ben-* generally have good connotations. *Malignant* and *benign* are often used to describe tumors or physical conditions that are either life-threatening or not.

cards.definition: to pretend to be sick to avoid doing work
cards.example:
Indolent Leon always *malingered* when it was his turn to clean up the house.
Arthur is artful, and he always manages to *malinger* before a big exam.

cards.definition: easy to shape or bend
cards.example: Modeling clay is very *malleable*. So is Stuart. We can make him do whatever we want him to do.

cards.definition: a command or authorization to do something; the will of the voters as expressed by the results of an election
cards.example:
Our *mandate* from the executive committee was to find the answer to the problem as quickly as possible.
The newly elected president felt that the landslide vote had given him a *mandate* to do whatever he wanted to do.
cards.notes:
= command to do something
*Mandate* can also be a verb. To *mandate* something is to command or require it.
A closely related word is *mandatory*, which means required or obligatory.

cards.definition: visible; evident
cards.example:
Daryl’s anger at us was *manifest:* You could see it in his expression and hear it in his voice.
Lee has been sick for a very long time, but it was only recently that he began to *manifest* symptoms.
Rebecca *manifested* alarm when we told her that the end of her ponytail was dipped into the bucket of paint.
cards.notes:
There is *manifest* danger in riding a pogo stick along the edge of a cliff.
*Manifest* can also be a verb, in which case it means to show, to make visible, or to make evident.
A visible sign of something is called a *manifestation* of it. A lack of comfort and luxury is the most obvious *manifestation* of poverty.

cards.definition: a public declaration of beliefs or principles, usually political ones
cards.example: Jim’s article about the election was less a piece of reporting than a *manifesto* of his political views.
cards.notes: The *Communist Manifesto* was a document that spelled out Karl Marx’s vision of a Communist world.

cards.definition: to arrange in order; to gather together for the purpose of doing something
cards.example:
The statistician *marshaled* his facts numerous times before making his presentation.
The general *marshaled* his troops in anticipation of making an attack on the enemy fortress.
We *marshaled* half a dozen local groups in opposition to the city council’s plan to bulldoze our neighborhood.

cards.definition: warlike; having to do with combat
cards.example:
The parade of soldiers was *martial* in tone; the soldiers carried rifles and were followed by a formation of tanks.
The school principal declared *martial* law when food riots erupted in the cafeteria.
cards.notes:
*Martial* is often confused with *marital* (MAR ih tul), which means having to do with marriage. Marriages are sometimes *martial*, but don’t confuse these words.
Karate and judo are often referred to as *martial* arts.

cards.definition: someone who gives up his or her life in pursuit of a cause, especially a religious one; one who suffers for a cause; one who makes a show of suffering in order to arouse sympathy
cards.example:
Jacob is a *martyr* to his job; he would stay at his desk twenty-four hours a day if his wife and the janitor would let him.
Eloise played the *martyr* during hay-fever season, trudging wearily from room to room with a jumbo box of Kleenex in each hand.
cards.notes:
= one who dies for a cause
Many of the saints were also *martyrs;* they were executed, often gruesomely, for refusing to renounce their religious beliefs.

cards.definition: to enroll, especially at a college
cards.example: Benny told everyone he was going to Harvard, but he actually *matriculated* to the local junior college.

cards.definition: silly and overly sentimental
cards.example:
The high school reunion grew more and more *maudlin* as the participants shared more and more memories.
Magdalen had a *maudlin* concern for the worms in her yard; she would bang a gong before walking in the grass in order to give them a chance to get out of her way.

cards.definition: a nonconformist; a rebel
cards.example:
The political scientist was an intellectual *maverick;* most of his theories had no followers except himself.
The *maverick* police officer got in trouble with the department for using illegal means to track down criminals.
cards.notes: *Maverick* can also be an adjective.

cards.definition: a fundamental principle; an old saying
cards.example:
We always tried to live our lives according to the *maxim* that it is better to give than to receive.
No one in the entire world is entirely certain of the differences in meaning among the words *maxim, adage, proverb*, and *aphorism*.

cards.definition: to help settle differences
cards.example:
The United Nations representative tried to *mediate* between the warring countries, but the soldiers just kept shooting at one another.
Joe carried messages back and forth between the divorcing husband and wife in the hope of *mediating* their differences.
cards.notes: To *mediate* is to engage in *mediation*. When two opposing groups, such as a trade union and the management of a company, try to settle their differences through *mediation*, they call in a *mediator* to listen to their cases and to make an equitable decision.

cards.definition: sweetly flowing
cards.example: Melanie’s clarinet playing was *mellifluous;* the notes flowed smoothly and beautifully.
cards.notes: *Mellifluous* comes from Greek words meaning, roughly, “honey flowing.” We use the word almost exclusively to describe voices, music, or sounds that flow sweetly, like honey.

cards.definition: lying; dishonest
cards.example: The jury saw through the *mendacious* witness and convicted the defendant.
cards.notes:
Thieves are naturally *mendacious*. If you ask them what they are doing, they will automatically answer, “Nothing.”
To be *mendacious* is to engage in *mendacity*, or lying. I have no flaws, except occasional *mendacity*. Don’t confuse this word with *mendicant*, listed below.

cards.definition: a beggar
cards.example: The presence of thousands of *mendicants* in every urban area is a sad commentary on our national priorities.

cards.definition: a teacher, tutor, counselor, or coach; especially in business, an experienced person who shows an inexperienced person the ropes
cards.example:
Chris’s *mentor* in the pole vault was a former track star who used to hang out by the gym and give the students pointers.
Young men and women in business often talk about the importance of having a *mentor*—usually an older person at the same company who takes an interest in them and helps them get ahead by showing them the ropes.
cards.notes: *Mentor* is too big a word to apply to just any teacher. A student might have many teachers but only one *mentor*—the person who taught him what was really important.

cards.definition: a hired soldier; someone who will do anything for money
cards.example:
Our business contains a few dedicated workers and many, many *mercenaries*, who want to make a quick buck and then get out.
Larry’s motives in writing the screenplay for the trashy movie were strictly *mercenary*—he needed the money.
cards.notes:
If an army can’t find enough volunteers or draftees, it will sometimes hire *mercenaries*. The magazine *Soldier of Fortune* is aimed at *mercenaries* and would-be *mercenaries;* it even runs classified advertisements by soldiers looking for someone to fight.
You don’t have to be a soldier to be a *mercenary*. Someone who does something strictly for the money is often called a *mercenary*.
*Mercenary* can also be used as an adjective.

cards.definition: emotionally unpredictable; rapidly changing in mood
cards.notes:
A person with a *mercurial* personality is one who changes rapidly and unpredictably between one mood and another.
*• Mercurial* Helen was crying one minute, laughing the next.

cards.definition: a magical change in form; a striking or sudden change
cards.example:
When the magician passed his wand over Eileen’s head, she underwent a bizarre *metamorphosis:* She turned into a hamster.
Damon’s *metamorphosis* from college student to Hollywood superstar was so sudden that it seemed a bit unreal.
cards.notes: To undergo a *metamorphosis* is to *metamorphose*.

cards.definition: the world in miniature
cards.example: Our community, which holds so many different communities, institutions, businesses, and types of people, is a microcosm of the larger world.
cards.notes:
The *cosmos* is the heavens, *cosmopolitan* means worldly, and a *microcosm is* a miniature version of the world. All three words are related.
The opposite of *microcosm* is a *macrocosm* (MAK ruh kahz um). A *macrocosm* is a large-scale representation of something, or the universe at large.

cards.definition: environment; surroundings
cards.example:
A caring and involved community is the proper *milieu* for raising a family.
The farmer on vacation in the big city felt out of his *milieu*.

cards.definition: very tiny
cards.example: Hank’s salary was *minuscule*, but the benefits were pretty good: He got to sit next to the refrigerator and eat all day long.
cards.notes:
Be careful with the spelling of this word. People tend to spell it “miniscule.” Think of *minus*.
*Minute* (mye NOOT) is a synonym for *minuscule*. The small details of something are the *minutiae* (mi NOO shi ee).

cards.definition: hating mankind
cards.notes: A *misogynist* (mis AH juh nist) hates women. A *misanthropic* person doesn’t make distinctions; he or she hates everyone. The opposite of a *misanthrope* (MIS un throhp) is a *philanthropist* (fuh LAN thruh pist). Curiously, there is no word for someone who hates men only.

cards.definition: to moderate the effect of something
cards.example:
The sense of imminent disaster was *mitigated* by the guide’s calm behavior and easy smile.
The effects of the disease were *mitigated* by the experimental drug treatment.
Nothing Joel said could *mitigate* the enormity of forgetting his mother-in-law’s birthday.
cards.notes: *Unmitigated* means absolute, unmoderated, not made less intense or severe.

cards.definition: to soften; to soothe; to pacify
cards.example:
Lucy *mollified* the angry police officer by kissing his hand.
My father was not *mollified* by my promise never to crash his car into a brick wall again.
The baby-sitter was unable to *mollify* the cranky child, who cried all night.

cards.definition: massive, solid, uniform, and unyielding
cards.notes:
= massive and unyielding
A *monolith* is a huge stone shaft or column. Many other things can be said to be *monolithic*.
A huge corporation is often said to be *monolithic*, especially if it is enormous and powerful and all its parts are dedicated to the same purpose.
If the opposition to a plan were said to be *monolithic*, it would probably consist of a large group of people who all felt the same way.

cards.definition: dying
cards.example:
The steel industry in this country was *moribund* a few years ago, but now it seems to be reviving somewhat.
The senator’s political ideas were *moribund;* no one thinks that way anymore.
cards.notes: A dying creature could be said to be *moribund*, too, although this word is usually used in connection with things that die only figuratively.

cards.definition: gloomy; sullen
cards.example:
Louise was always so *morose* about everything that she was never any fun to be with.
New Yorkers always seemed *morose* to the writer who lived in the country; he thought they seemed beaten down by the city.

cards.definition: to humiliate
cards.example:
I was *mortified* when my father asked my girlfriend whether she thought I was a dumb, pathetic wimp.
We had a *mortifying* experience at the opera; when Stanley’s cell phone rang, the entire orchestra stopped playing and stared at him for several minutes.

cards.definition: ordinary; pretty boring; not heavenly and eternal
cards.example:
My day was filled with *mundane* chores: I mowed the lawn, did the laundry, and fed the dog.
Dee’s job was so *mundane* she sometimes had trouble remembering whether she was at work or asleep.
The monk’s thoughts were far removed from *mundane* concerns; he was contemplating all the fun he was going to have in heaven.

cards.definition: very generous; lavish
cards.example:
The *munificent* millionaire gave lots of money to any charity that came to him with a request.
Mrs. Bigelow was a *munificent* hostess; there was so much wonderful food and wine at her dinner parties that the guests had to rest between courses. She was known for her *munificence*.

cards.definition: nearsightedness; lack of foresight
cards.example:
The president suffered from economic *myopia;* he was unable to see the consequences of his fiscal policies.
The workers’ dissatisfaction was inflamed by management’s *myopia* on the subject of wages.
cards.notes:
*Myopia* is the fancy medical name for the inability to see clearly at a distance. It’s also a word used in connection with people who lack other kinds of visual acuity.
To suffer myopia is to be *myopic* (mye AHP ik). Some people who wear glasses are *myopic*. So are the people who can’t see the consequences of their actions.

cards.definition: a huge number
cards.example:
A country sky on a clear night is filled with a *myriad* of stars.
There are a *myriad* of reasons why I don’t like school.
cards.notes: This word can also be used as an adjective. *Myriad* stars is a lot of stars. The teenager was weighted down by the *myriad* anxieties of adolescence.

cards.definition: excessive love of one’s body or oneself
cards.example:
In Greek mythology, Narcissus was a boy who fell in love with his own reflection. To engage in *narcissism* is to be like Narcissus.
Throwing a kiss to your reflection in the mirror is an act of *narcissism*—so is filling your living room with all your bowling trophies or telling everyone how smart and good-looking you are. You are a *narcissist* (NAHR suh sist).
The selfish students were bound up in *narcissistic* concerns and gave no thought to other people.
cards.notes:
= excessive love of self
Someone who suffers from *narcissism* is said to be *narcissistic* (nahr si SIS tik).

cards.definition: vague; hazy; indistinct
cards.example:
Oscar’s views are so *nebulous* that no one can figure out what he thinks about anything.
The community’s boundaries are somewhat *nebulous;* where they are depends on whom you ask.
Molly’s expensive new hairdo was a sort of *nebulous* mass of wisps, waves, and hair spray.
cards.notes: A *nebula* (NEB yuh luh) is an interstellar cloud, the plural of which is *nebulae* (NEB yuh lee).

cards.definition: evil; flagrantly wicked
cards.example:
The radicals’ *nefarious* plot was to destroy New York by filling the reservoirs with strawberry Jell-O.
The convicted murderer had committed a myriad of *nefarious* acts.

cards.definition: a new word or phrase; a new usage of a word
cards.notes: Pedants don’t like *neologisms*. They like the words we already have. But at one time every word was a *neologism*. Someone somewhere had to be the first to use it.

cards.definition: showing favoritism to friends or family in business or politics
cards.example: Clarence had no business acumen, so he was counting on *nepotism* when he married the boss’s daughter.

cards.definition: the belief that there are no values or morals in the universe
cards.example: A *nihilist* does not believe in any objective standards of right or wrong.
cards.notes: = belief in the absence of all values and morals

cards.definition: in name only; insignificant; A-OK (during rocket launches)
cards.example:
Bert was the *nominal* chair of the committee, but Sue was the one who ran things.
The cost was *nominal* in comparison with the enormous value of what you received.
“All systems are *nominal*,” said the NASA engineer as the space shuttle successfully headed into orbit.

cards.definition: sentimental longing for the past; homesickness
cards.example:
A wave of *nostalgia* overcame me when the old Biggie Smalls song came on the radio; hearing it took me right back to 1997.
Some people who don’t remember what the decade was really like feel a misplaced *nostalgia* for the 1950s.
As we talked about the fun we’d had together in junior high school, we all began to feel a little *nostalgic*.
cards.notes: To be filled with *nostalgia* is to be *nostalgic*.

cards.definition: famous for something bad
cards.example:
No one wanted to play poker with Jeremy because he was a *notorious* cheater.
Rana’s practical jokes were *notorious;* people always kept their distance when she came into the room.
Jesse’s *notoriety* as a bank robber made it difficult for him to find a job in banking.
cards.notes:
A well-known actor is famous; a well-known criminal is *notorious*.
To be *notorious* is to have *notoriety* (noh tuh RYE uh tee).

cards.definition: new; original
cards.example:
Ray had a *novel* approach to homework: He did the work before the teacher assigned it.
There was nothing *novel* about the author’s latest novel; the characters were old, and the plot was borrowed.

cards.definition: harmful; offensive
cards.example:
Smoking is a *noxious* habit in every sense.
Poison ivy is a *noxious* weed.
The mothers’ committee believed that rock ‘n’ roll music exerted a *noxious* influence on their children.

cards.definition: a subtle difference or distinction
cards.example:
The artist’s best work explored the *nuance* between darkness and deep shadow.
Harry was incapable of *nuance;* everything for him was either black or white.
cards.notes: In certain Chinese dialects, the difference between one word and its opposite is sometimes nothing more than a *nuance* of inflection.

cards.definition: stubborn and insensitive
cards.example:
The committee’s *obdurate* refusal to listen to our plan was heartbreaking to us since we had spent ten years coming up with it.
The child begged and begged to have the bubble-gum machine installed in his bedroom, but his parents were *obdurate* in their insistence that it should go in the kitchen.
cards.notes: *Obdurate* contains one of the same roots as *durable* and *endurance;* each word conveys a different sense of hardness.

cards.definition: to darken; to confuse; to make confusing
cards.example:
The spokesman’s attempt to explain what the president had meant merely *obfuscated* the issue further. People had hoped the spokesman would elucidate the issue.
Too much gin had *obfuscated* the old man’s senses.
The professor’s inept lecture gradually *obfuscated* a subject that had been crystal clear to us before.
Lester called himself a used-car salesman, but his real job was *obfuscation:* He sold cars by confusing his customers.
cards.notes: To *obfuscate* something is to engage in *obfuscation*.

cards.definition: indirect; at an angle
cards.example: Essence sprinkled her student council speech with *oblique* references to the principal’s new toupee; the principal is so dense that he never figured out what was going on, but the rest of us were rolling on the floor.
cards.notes:
In geometry, lines are said to be *oblique* if they are neither parallel nor perpendicular to one another. The word has a related meaning outside of mathematics. An *oblique* statement is one that does not directly address the topic at hand, that approaches it as if from an angle.
An allusion could be said to be an *oblique* reference. An *oblique* argument is one that does not directly confront its true subject.
To insult someone *obliquely* is to do so indirectly.

cards.definition: total forgetfulness; the state of being forgotten
cards.example:
A few of the young actors would find fame, but most were headed for *oblivion*.
After tossing and turning with anxiety for most of the night, Marisol finally found the *oblivion* of sleep.
Old age had made the retired professor *oblivious* of all his old theories.
The workmen stomped in and out of the room, but the happy child, playing on the floor, was *oblivious* of all distraction.
cards.notes:
To be *oblivious* is to be forgetful or unaware.
It is also acceptable to say “*oblivious* to” rather than “*oblivious* of.”

cards.definition: unknown; hard to understand; dark
cards.example:
The comedy nightclub was filled with *obscure* comedians who stole one another’s jokes and seldom got any laughs.
The artist was so *obscure* that even his parents had trouble remembering his name.
The noted scholar’s dissertation was terribly *obscure;* it had to be translated from English into English before anyone could make head or tail of it.
Some contemporary poets apparently believe that the only way to be great is to be *obscure*.
The details of the forest grew *obscure* as night fell.
cards.notes: The state of being *obscure* in any of its senses is called *obscurity*.

cards.definition: fawning; subservient; sucking up to
cards.example:
Ann’s assistant was so *obsequious* that she could never tell what he really thought about anything.
My *obsequious* friend seemed to live only to make me happy and never wanted to do anything if I said I didn’t want to do it.

cards.definition: insensitive; blockheaded
cards.example:
Karen was so *obtuse* that she didn’t realize for several days that Caleb had asked her to marry him.
The *obtuse* student couldn’t seem to grasp the difference between addition and subtraction.

cards.definition: annoyingly eager to help or advise
cards.example:
The *officious* officer could never resist sticking his nose into other people’s business.
The *officious* salesperson refused to leave us alone, so we finally left without buying anything.
cards.notes: = annoyingly helpful

cards.definition: burdensome; oppressive
cards.example:
We were given the *onerous* task of cleaning up the fairgrounds after the carnival.
The job had long hours, but the work wasn’t *onerous;* Bill spent most of his time sitting with his feet on the desk.
cards.notes: This word can be pronounced “OH nur us.”

cards.definition: impossible to see through; impossible to understand
cards.example:
The windows in the movie star’s house were made not of glass but of some *opaque* material intended to keep his fans from spying on him.
We tried to figure out what Horace was thinking, but his expression was *opaque:* It revealed nothing.
Jerry’s mind, assuming he had one, was *opaque*.
The statement was *opaque;* no one could make anything of it.
cards.notes: The noun form of *opaque* is *opacity* (oh PAS uh tee).

cards.definition: luxurious
cards.example:
Everything in the *opulent* palace was made of gold—except the toilet-paper holder, which was made of platinum.
The investment banker had grown so accustomed to an *opulent* lifestyle that he had trouble adjusting to the federal penitentiary.
cards.notes: *Opulence* is often ostentatious.

cards.definition: conventional; adhering to established principles or doctrines, especially in religion; by the book
cards.example:
The doctor’s treatment for Lou’s cold was entirely *orthodox:* plenty of liquids, aspirin, and rest.
Austin’s views were *orthodox;* there was nothing shocking about any of them.
The teacher’s lectures were characterized by strict adherence to *orthodoxy*.
“Swiss cheese” is an *unorthodox* explanation for the composition of the moon.
cards.notes:
The body of what is *orthodox* is called *orthodoxy*.
To be unconventional is to be *unorthodox*.

cards.definition: apparent (but misleading); professed
cards.example:
Blake’s *ostensible* mission was to repair a broken telephone, but his real goal was to eavesdrop on the boss’s conversation.
Trevor’s *ostensible* kindness to squirrels belied his deep hatred of them.
cards.notes: = misleading apparent

cards.definition: excessively conspicuous; showing off
cards.example:
The designer’s use of expensive materials was *ostentatious;* every piece of furniture was covered with silk or velvet, and every piece of hardware was made of silver or gold.
The donor was *ostentatious* in making his gift to the hospital. He held a big press conference to announce it and then walked through the wards to give patients an opportunity to thank him personally.
The young lawyer had *ostentatiously* hung his Harvard diploma on the door to his office.
Lamar wore solid-gold shoes to the party; I was shocked by his *ostentation*.
cards.notes: To be *ostentatious* is to engage in *ostentation*.

cards.definition: to calm someone down; to placate
cards.notes: A parent gives a baby a *pacifier* to *pacify* him or her. A *pacifist* is someone who does not believe in war.

cards.definition: extremely careful; taking pains *Painstaking* = pains-taking = taking pains.
cards.example: The jeweler was *painstaking* in his effort not to ruin the $50 million diamond necklace.

cards.definition: to relieve or alleviate something without getting rid of the problem; to assuage; to mitigate
cards.example: You take aspirin in the hope that it will *palliate* your headache.
cards.notes: Aspirin is a *palliative* (PAL yuh tiv).

cards.definition: capable of being touched; obvious; tangible
cards.example:
The tumor was *palpable;* the doctor could feel it with his finger.
Harry’s disappointment at being rejected by every college in America was *palpable;* it was so obvious that you could almost reach out and touch it.
There was *palpable* danger in flying the kite in a thunderstorm.
cards.notes: The opposite of *palpable* is *impalpable*.

cards.definition: insignificant; worthless
cards.example:
The lawyer’s efforts on our behalf were *paltry;* they didn’t add up to anything.
The *paltry* fee he paid us was scarcely large enough to cover our expenses.

cards.definition: something that cures everything
cards.example:
The administration seemed to believe that a tax cut would be a *panacea* for the country’s economic ills.
Granny believed that her “rheumatiz medicine” was a *panacea*. No matter what you were sick with, that was what she prescribed.
cards.notes: = cure for everything

cards.definition: a model or example
cards.example:
Mr. Hufstader is the best teacher in the whole world; his classroom should be the *paradigm* for all classrooms.
In selecting her wardrobe, messy Ana apparently used a scarecrow as her *paradigm*.
Virtually all the cars the company produced were based on a single, *paradigmatic* design.
cards.notes: A *paradigm* is *paradigmatic* (par uh dig MAT ik).

cards.definition: a true statement or phenomenon that nonetheless seems to contradict itself; an untrue statement or phenomenon that nonetheless seems logical
cards.example:
Mr. Cooper is a political *paradox;* he’s a staunch Republican who votes only for Democrats.
One of Xeno’s *paradoxes* seems to prove the impossibility of an arrow’s ever reaching its target: If the arrow first moves half the distance to the target, then half the remaining distance, then half the remaining distance, and so on, it can never arrive.
Pasquale’s dislike of ice cream was *paradoxical* considering that he worked as an ice-cream taster.
cards.notes:
= contradictory truth
A *paradox* is *paradoxical*.

cards.definition: narrow or confined in point of view; provincial
cards.example:
The townspeople’s concerns were entirely *parochial;* they worried only about what happened in their town and not about the larger world around it.
The journalist’s *parochial* point of view prevented him from becoming a nationally known figure.
cards.notes:
= narrow in point of view
A lot of people think a *parochial* school is a religious school. Traditionally, a *parochial* school is just the school of the parish or neighborhood. In other contexts *parochial* has negative connotations.

cards.definition: a satirical imitation
cards.example:
At the talent show the girls sang a terrible *parody* of a Beatles song called “I Want to Hold Your Foot.”
The unhappy student accused Mr. Benson of being not a teacher but a *parody* of one.
cards.notes:
Some *parodies* are unintentional and not very funny.
*Parody* can also be a verb. To *parody* something is to make a *parody* of it. A *parody* is *parodic* (puh ROD ik).

cards.definition: stingy
cards.example:
The widow was so *parsimonious* that she hung used teabags out to dry on her clothesline so that she would be able to use them again.
We tried to be *parsimonious*, but without success. After just a few days at the resort we realized we had spent all the money we had set aside for our entire month-long vacation.
cards.notes: To be *parsimonious* is to practice *parsimony*.

cards.definition: one who supports a particular person, cause, or idea
cards.example:
Henry’s plan to give himself the award had no *partisan* except himself.
I am the *partisan* of any candidate who promises not to make promises.
The mountain village was attacked by *partisans* of the rebel chieftain.
Both the Republican and Democratic senators voted to give themselves a raise. The motion had *bipartisan* support.
cards.notes:
= supporter of a cause
*Partisan* can also be used as an adjective meaning biased, as in *partisan* politics. An issue that everyone agrees on regardless of the party he or she belongs to is a *nonpartisan* issue. *Bipartisan* means supported by two (bi) parties.

cards.definition: obvious
cards.example:
To say that the earth is flat is a *patent* absurdity since the world is obviously spherical.
It was *patently* foolish of Lee to think that he could sail across the Pacific Ocean in a washtub.

cards.definition: fatherly; fatherlike
cards.example: Rich is *paternal* toward his niece.
cards.notes: *Maternal* (muh TUR nul) means motherly or momlike.

cards.definition: the science of diseases
cards.notes: *Pathology* is the science or study of diseases, but not necessarily in the medical sense. *Pathological* means relating to *pathology*, but it also means arising from a disease. So if we say Brad is an inveterate, incorrigible, *pathological* (path uh LAHJ uh kul) liar, we are saying that Brad’s lying is a sickness.

cards.definition: the male head of a family or tribe
cards.example:
The *patriarch* of the Murphy family, Jacob V. Murphy, made millions selling cobra fillets and established the Murphy family’s empire in the snake meat business.
In the *patriarchal* country of Spambulia, the ruling monarch can never be a woman, though the current king is such a numbskull that his sister runs things behind the scenes.
Spambulia is considering becoming a *matriarchy* (MAY tree ahr kee).
cards.notes:
The adjective is *patriarchal* (pay tree AHRK ul).
A female head of a family is a *matriarch*, and such a family would be described as *matriarchal*.

cards.definition: a person of noble birth; an aristocrat
cards.example:
Mr. Perno was a *patrician*, and he was never truly happy unless his place at the dinner table was set with at least half a dozen forks.
The noisy crowd on the luxury ocean liner was *patrician* in dress but not in behavior; they were wearing tuxedos but throwing deck chairs into the ocean.
cards.notes: *Patrician* can also be an adjective. Polo is a *patrician* sport.

cards.definition: to treat as an inferior; to condescend to
cards.example:
Our guide at the art gallery was extremely *patronizing*, treating us as though we wouldn’t be able to distinguish a painting from a piece of sidewalk without her help.
We felt *patronized* by the waiter at the fancy restaurant; he ignored all our efforts to attract his attention and then pretended not to understand our accents.
