When a writer or speaker “goes off on a *tangent*,” he or she is making a digression or straying from the original topic.

cards.definition: touchable; palpable
cards.example:
A mountain of cigarette butts was the only *tangible* evidence that Luke had been in our house.
There was no *tangible* reason I could point to, but I did have a sneaking suspicion that Ernest was a rodeo fan.
cards.notes: The opposite of *tangible* is *intangible*.

cards.definition: equivalent to
cards.example:
Waving a banner for the visiting team at that football game would be *tantamount* to committing suicide; the home-team fans would tear you apart in a minute.
Yvonne’s method of soliciting donations from her employees was *tantamount* to extortion; she clearly implied that she would fire them if they didn’t pitch in.

cards.definition: redundant; circular
cards.example:
The testing company’s definition of intelligence—“that which is measured by intelligence tests”—is *tautological*.
The trouble with bachelors is that they aren’t married.
cards.notes:
“When everyone has a camera, cameras will be universal” is a *tautological* statement, because “everyone having a camera” and “cameras being universal” mean the same thing.
A *tautology* (taw TAHL uh jee) is a needless repetition of words, or saying the same thing using different words. For example:

cards.definition: boldness; recklessness; audacity
cards.example:
Our waiter at the restaurant had the *temerity* to tell me he thought my table manners were atrocious.
The mountain climber had more *temerity* than skill or sense. He tried to climb a mountain that was much too difficult and ended up in a heap at the bottom.

cards.definition: mild; moderate; restrained
cards.example:
Our climate is *temperate* during the spring and fall but nearly unbearable during the summer and winter.
The teacher’s *temperate* personality lent a feeling of calm and control to the kindergarten class.
Becky’s *intemperate* use of oregano ruined the chili.
Anna laughed and shrieked so loudly at every joke that even the comedian wished she would *temper* her appreciation.
cards.notes:
The opposite of *temperate* is *intemperate*, which means not moderate.
To *temper* something is to make it milder.
*Temperance* is moderation, especially with regard to alcoholic drinks.

cards.definition: defensible, as in one’s position in an argument; capable of being argued successfully; valid
cards.example: Members of the Flat Earth Society continue to argue that the earth is flat, although even children dismiss their arguments as *untenable*.
cards.notes: *Untenable* means unable to be defended.

cards.definition: persistent; stubborn; not letting go
cards.example:
The foreign student’s *tenacious* effort to learn English won him the admiration of all the teachers at our school.
Louise’s grasp of geometry was not *tenacious*. She could handle the simpler problems most of the time, but she fell apart on quizzes and tests.
The ivy growing on the side of our house was so *tenacious* that we had to tear the house down to get rid of it.
cards.notes: To be *tenacious* is to have *tenacity* (tuh NAS us tee).

cards.definition: a shared principle or belief
cards.example:
The *tenets* of his religion prohibited him from dancing and going to movies.
One of the most important *tenets* of our form of government is that people can be trusted to govern themselves.

cards.definition: experimental; temporary; uncertain
cards.example:
George made a *tentative* effort to paint his house by himself; he slapped some paint on the front door and his clothes, tipped over the bucket, and called a professional.
Our plans for the party are *tentative* at this point, but we are considering hiring a troupe of accordionists to play polkas while our guests are eating dessert.
Hugo believed himself to be a great wit, but his big joke was rewarded by nothing more than a very *tentative* chuckle from his audience.

cards.definition: flimsy; extremely thin
cards.example:
The organization’s financial situation has always been *tenuous;* the balance of the checking account is usually close to zero.
Cherrie admitted that she stole the Cracker Jacks, but claimed that there were *extenuating* circumstances: She had no money to buy food for her dog.
cards.notes: To *attenuate* is to make thin. *Extenuating* circumstances are those that lessen the magnitude of something, especially a crime.

cards.definition: using no unnecessary words; succinct
cards.example:
The new recording secretary’s minutes were so *terse* that they were occasionally cryptic.
*Terseness* is not one of Rex’s virtues; he would talk until the crack of dawn if someone didn’t stop him.
cards.notes: = without unnecessary words

cards.definition: the study of God or religion
cards.example: Ralph was a paradox: He was an atheist, yet he passionately studied *theology*.
cards.notes: = study of religion

cards.definition: a prolonged, bitter speech
cards.example: Preston launched into a *tirade* against imitation cheese on the school lunch menu.

cards.definition: sluggishness; inactivity; apathy
cards.example:
After consuming the guinea pig, the boa constrictor fell into a state of contented *torpor* that lasted several days.
The math teacher tried to reduce the *torpor* of his students by banging on his desk, but the students scarcely blinked.
cards.notes: To be in a state of *torpor* is to be *torpid*.

cards.definition: a standard; a test of authenticity or quality
cards.example:
The size of a student’s vocabulary is a useful *touchstone* for judging the quality of his or her education.
A candidate’s pronouncements about the economy provided a *touchstone* by which his or her fitness for office could be judged.
cards.notes: In its original usage, a *touchstone* was a dark stone against which gold and other precious metals were rubbed in order to test their purity. Now the word is used more loosely to describe a broad range of standards and tests.

cards.definition: to praise highly; to brag publicly about
cards.example: Advertisements *touted* the chocolate-flavored toothpaste as getting rid of your sweet tooth while saving your teeth.

cards.definition: to go beyond or above; to surpass
cards.example:
The man who claimed to have invented a perpetual motion machine believed that he had *transcended* the laws of physics.
The basketball player was so skillful that she seemed to have *transcended* the sport altogether; she was so much better than her teammates that she seemed to be playing an entirely different game.
cards.notes: To be *transcendent* is to be surpassing or preeminent. Something *transcendent* is *transcendental* (tran sen DEN tul).

cards.definition: to violate (a law); to sin
cards.example:
The other side had *transgressed* so many provisions of the treaty that we had no choice but to go to war.
We tried as hard as we could not to *transgress* their elaborate rules, but they had so many prohibitions that we couldn’t keep track of all of them.
The bully’s innumerable *transgressions* included breaking all the windows in the new gymnasium and pushing several first graders off the jungle gym.
cards.notes: An act of *transgressing* is a *transgression*.

cards.definition: not staying for a long time; temporary
cards.example:
The *transient* breeze provided some relief from the summer heat, but we were soon perspiring again.
The child’s smile was *transient;* it disappeared as soon as the candy bar was gone.
A hotel’s inhabitants are *transient;* they come and go, and the population changes every night.
cards.notes:
= not lasting long
*Transient* can also be a noun. A *transient* person is sometimes called a *transient*. Hoboes, mendicants, and other homeless people are often called *transients*.
A very similar word is *transitory*, which means not lasting long. A *transient* breeze might provide *transitory* relief from the heat.
This word can also be pronounced “TRAN zee unt.”

cards.definition: fear; apprehension; nervous trembling
cards.example:
The nursery school students were filled with *trepidation* when they saw the other children in their class dressed in their Halloween costumes.
The *trepidation* of the swimming team was readily apparent: Their knees were knocking as they lined up along the edge of the pool.
The *intrepid* captain sailed his ship around the world with only a handkerchief for a sail.
cards.notes: To be fearless is to be *intrepid*.

cards.definition: shameful wickedness; depravity
cards.example: Paul was sacked by his boss because of a flagrant act of *turpitude:* He was caught stealing office supplies.

cards.definition: being everywhere at the same time
cards.example:
The new beer commercial was *ubiquitous*—it seemed to be on every television channel at once.
Personal computers, once a rarity, have become *ubiquitous*.
cards.notes:
= everywhere at once
To be *ubiquitous* is to be characterized by *ubiquity* (yoo BIK wuh tee). The *ubiquity* of fast-food restaurants is one of the more depressing features of American culture.

cards.definition: not controlled by conscience; unscrupulous
cards.example:
Leaving a small child unattended all day long is an *unconscionable* act.
Stealing money from every citizen of that town was *unconscionable*. Bert should be ashamed of himself for doing it.
cards.notes: Don’t confuse this word with *unconscious*.

cards.definition: oily, both literally and figuratively; insincere
cards.notes:
= oily; slick
Salad oil is literally *unctuous*. A used-car salesman might be figuratively *unctuous*—that is, oily in the sense of being slick, sleazy, and insincere.

cards.definition: consistent; unchanging; the same for everyone
cards.example:
Traffic laws are similar from one state to the next, but they aren’t *uniform;* each state has its own variations.
The school did not have a *uniform* grading policy; each teacher was free to mark students according to any system that he or she thought appropriate.
cards.notes:
Something that is *uniform* has *uniformity* (yoo nuh FOR muh tee).
*Uniforms* are suits of clothing that are *uniform* in appearance from one person to the next.

cards.definition: unceasing; unabated; relentless
cards.example: Superman waged an *unremitting* battle against evildoers everywhere.

cards.definition: unintentional; ignorant; not aware
cards.example:
When Leo agreed to hold open the door of the bank, he became an *unwitting* accomplice to the bank robbery.
My theft was *unwitting;* I hadn’t meant to steal the car, but had absentmindedly driven it away from the automobile dealership and parked it in my garage.
On the camping trip, Josephine *unwittingly* stepped into a bear trap and remained stuck in it for several days.

cards.definition: poised; sophisticated; refined
cards.example:
The British count was witty and *urbane;* all the hosts and hostesses wanted to have him at their parties.
The new magazine was far too *urbane* to appeal to a wide audience outside the big city.
cards.notes:
= poised and sophisticated
*Urbanity* (ur BAN uh tee) is a quality more often acquired in an *urban* setting than in a rural one.

cards.definition: to seize wrongfully
cards.example:
The children believed that their mother’s new boyfriend had *usurped* their father’s rightful place in their family.
The founder’s scheming young nephew *usurped* a position of power in the company.
cards.notes: The noun is *usurpation* (yoo sur PAY shun).

cards.pron: yoo til uh TAR ee un
cards.definition: stressing usefulness or utility above all other qualities; pragmatic
cards.example: Jason’s interior-decorating philosophy was strictly *utilitarian;* if an object wasn’t genuinely useful, he didn’t want it in his home.
cards.notes: *Utilitarian* can also be a noun. Jason, just aforementioned, could be called a *utilitarian*.

cards.definition: an ideal society
cards.example:
A country where nobody had to work would be Quentin’s idea of *utopia*.
The little town wasn’t just a nice place to live, as far as Ed was concerned; it was *utopia*.
cards.notes:
A *utopian* is someone with unrealistic or impractical plans or expectations for society. Such plans or expectations are *utopian* plans or expectations.
The opposite of a *utopia* is a *dystopia*.

cards.definition: to be indecisive; to waver
cards.example:
We invited James to spend Thanksgiving with us, but he *vacillated* for so long that we finally became annoyed and disinvited him.
Tyler *vacillated* about buying a new car. He couldn’t decide whether to get one.
cards.notes: The act of *vacillating* is called *vacillation*.

cards.definition: without liveliness; dull; spiritless
cards.example: The novelist’s prose was so *vapid* that Mary couldn’t get beyond the first page.
cards.notes: An apathetic person just doesn’t care about anything, and everything he does is *vapid*.

cards.definition: intense; forceful; violent
cards.example: Shaking his fist and stomping his foot, Gerry was *vehement* in his denial.
cards.notes: The noun is *vehemence*.

cards.definition: capable of being bribed; willing to do anything for money; corrupt
cards.example:
The *venal* judge reversed his favorable ruling when the defendant refused to make good on his promised bribe.
The young man’s interest in helping the sick old woman was strictly *venal;* he figured that if he was kind to her, she would leave him a lot of money in her will.
cards.notes:
A *venal* person is a person characterized by *venality* (vee NAL uh tee).
Don’t confuse this word with *venial* (VEE nee ul), which means trivial or pardonable. A peccadillo is a *venial*, harmless sin.

cards.definition: to revere; to treat as something holy, especially because of great age
cards.example:
Lester *venerated* his grandfather; he worshiped the ground the old man limped on.
The members of the curious religion *venerated* Elvis Presley and hoped that the pope would declare him a saint.
cards.notes: A person who is worthy of being *venerated* is said to be *venerable*.

cards.definition: truthfulness
cards.example: The *veracity* of young George Washington is apocryphal.
cards.notes: *Veracious* (vuh RAY shus) means truthful.

cards.definition: using too many words; not succinct; circumlocutory
cards.example: Lee handed in a 178-word final assignment; no one ever accused him of *verbosity* (vur BAHS uh tee).
cards.notes:
= wordy
Someone who is *verbose* uses too many words when fewer words would suffice.

cards.pron: ver uh si MIL uh tood
cards.definition: similarity to reality; the appearance of truth; looking like the real thing
cards.example:
They used pine cones and old truck tires to make statues of Hollywood celebrities that were remarkable for their *verisimilitude*.
The *verisimilitude* of counterfeit eleven-dollar bills did not fool the eagle-eyed treasury officer, who recognized them immediately for what they were.

cards.definition: everyday speech; slang; idiom
cards.example: Our teacher said that we should save our *vernacular* for the street; in the classroom we should use proper grammar.

cards.definition: a remaining bit of something; a last trace
cards.example:
The unhappy young man found *vestiges* of his fiancée in the rubble, but the explosion had effectively ended their romance.
An old uniform and a tattered scrapbook were the only *vestiges* of the old man’s career as a professional athlete.
cards.notes:
Your appendix is a *vestige:* It used to have a function, but now this organ does nothing.
The adjective form of *vestige* is *vestigial* (vuh STIJ ee ul). The appendix is referred to as a *vestigial* organ. It is still in our bodies, although it no longer has a function. It is a mere *vestige* of some function our digestive systems no longer perform.

cards.definition: to annoy; to pester; to confuse
cards.example:
Margaret *vexed* me by poking me with a long, sharp stick.
Stuck at the bottom of a deep well, I found my situation extremely *vexing*.
cards.notes: The act of *vexing*, or the state of being *vexed*, is *vexation*. A *vexed* issue is one that is troubling or puzzling.

cards.definition: capable of living; workable
cards.example:
When a doctor says that an organ is no longer *viable*, it means it can’t be used as a transplant organ.
A fetus is said to be *viable* when it has developed to the point when it is capable of surviving outside the womb.
Lupe’s plan for storing marshmallows in the dome of the Capitol just wasn’t *viable*.
cards.notes: Something that is *viable* has *viability* (vye uh BIL uh tee).

cards.definition: experienced, performed, or suffered through someone else; living through the experiences of another as though they were one’s own experiences
cards.example: We all felt a *vicarious* thrill when the mayor’s daughter won fourth prize in the regional kickboxing competition.
cards.notes:
= experienced through another
To take *vicarious* pleasure in someone else’s success is to enjoy that person’s success as though it were your own.

cards.definition: upheaval; natural change; change in fortune
cards.example:
The *vicissitudes* of the stock market were too much for Karen; she decided to look for a job that would stay the same from one day to the next.
The *vicissitudes* of the local political machine were such that one could never quite be certain whom one was supposed to bribe.

cards.definition: to say vile things about; to defame
cards.example:
The teacher was reprimanded for *vilifying* the slow student in front of the rest of the class.
Our taxi driver paused briefly on the way to the airport to *vilify* the driver of the car that had nearly forced him off the road.
The political debate was less a debate than a *vilification* contest. At first the candidates took turns saying nasty things about one another; then they stopped taking turns.

cards.definition: to clear from all blame or suspicion; to justify
cards.example:
George, having been accused of stealing money from the cash register, was *vindicated* when the store manager counted the money again and found that none was missing after all.
Tom’s claim of innocence appeared to be *vindicated* when several dozen inmates at the state mental hospital confessed to the crime of which he had been accused.
cards.notes:
= clear from suspicion
A person who has been *vindicated* is a person who has found *vindication*.

cards.definition: seeking revenge
cards.example:
Jeremy apologized for denting the fender of my car, but I was feeling *vindictive*, so I made him buy me a new car.
Samantha’s *vindictive* ex drove all the way across the country just to put a stink bomb in her car.
cards.notes: To feel *vindictive* is to be filled with *vindictiveness*.

cards.definition: a masterful musician; a masterful practitioner in some other field
cards.example:
The concert audience fell silent when the *virtuoso* stepped forward to play the sonata on his electric banjo.
As an artist, he was a *virtuoso;* as a husband, he was a chump.
cards.notes: *Virtuoso* can also be an adjective. A *virtuoso* performance is a performance worthy of a *virtuoso*.

cards.definition: extremely poisonous; malignant; full of hate
cards.example:
The *virulent* disease quickly swept through the community, leaving many people dead and many more people extremely ill.
The snake was a member of a particularly *virulent* breed; its bite could kill an elephant.
Jonathan is a *virulent* antifeminist; he says that all women should sit down and shut up.
cards.notes: To be *virulent* is to be characterized by *virulence. Virulent* is related to *virus*, not to *virile*, which means manly.

cards.definition: a dreamer; someone with impractical goals or ideas about the future
cards.example:
My uncle was a *visionary*, not a businessman; he spent too much time tinkering with his antigravity generator and not enough time working for his plumbing business.
The candidate was a *visionary;* he had a lot of big ideas but no realistic plan for putting them into practice.
cards.notes: *Visionary* can also be an adjective. A *visionary* proposal is an idealistic and usually impractical proposal.

cards.definition: to make impure; to pollute
cards.example: For years a zealous group of individuals has campaigned against the use of fluoride in water, claiming that it has *vitiated* our bodies as well as our morals.

cards.definition: caustic; full of bitterness
cards.example: The review of the new book was so *vitriolic* that we all wondered whether the reviewer had some personal grudge against the author.
cards.notes: *Vitriol* is another name for sulfuric acid. To be *vitriolic* is to say or do something so nasty that your words or actions burn like acid.

cards.definition: an occupation; a job
cards.example:
If Stan could figure out how to make a *vocation* out of watching television and eating potato chips, he would be one of the most successful people in the world.
The accountant’s *vocation* bored her, but her *avocation* of mountain climbing did not.
cards.notes:
Your *vocation* is what you do for a living.
*Vocational* training is job training. Since your *vocation* is your job, your *avocation* is your hobby.

cards.definition: loud; noisy
cards.example: Randy often becomes *vociferous* during arguments. He doesn’t know what he believes, but he states it loudly nevertheless.

cards.definition: quick to evaporate; highly unstable; explosive
cards.example:
A *volatile* liquid is one that evaporates readily. Gasoline is a *volatile* liquid. It evaporates readily, and then the vapor poses a great danger of explosion.
A *volatile* crowd is one that seems to be in imminent danger of getting out of control or exploding.
The situation in the Middle East was highly *volatile;* the smallest incident could have set off a war.
cards.notes: To be *volatile* is to be characterized by *volatility*.

cards.definition: will; conscious choice
cards.example:
Insects, lacking *volition*, simply aren’t as interesting to the aspiring anthropologist as humans are.
The question the jury had to answer was whether the killing had been an accident or an act of *volition*.

cards.definition: malicious; unjustifiable; unprovoked; egregious
cards.example:
Terrorists commit *wanton* acts on a helpless populace to make their point.
A hedonist lives a *wanton* life in the relentless, unremitting pursuit of pleasure; an ascetic does not.
cards.notes: *Wanton* also means intemperate.

cards.definition: deliberate; obstinate; insistent on having one’s way
cards.example:
The mother insisted that the killing committed by her son had not been *willful*, but the jury apparently believed that he had known what he was doing.
When her mother told her she couldn’t have a cookie, the *willful* little girl simply snatched the cookie jar and ran out of the room with it. She had stolen the cookies *willfully*.

cards.definition: yearning; sadly longing
cards.example:
I felt *wistful* when I saw Steve’s fancy new car. I wished that I had enough money to buy one for myself.
The boys who had been cut from the football team watched *wistfully* as the team put together an undefeated season and won the state championship.

cards.definition: enthusiastically devoted to something; fervent
cards.example:
The *zealous* young policeman made so many arrests that the city jail soon became overcrowded.
The dictator’s followers were so *zealous* that if he had asked them all to jump off a cliff, most of them would have done so.
cards.notes: To be *zealous* is to be full of zeal, or fervent enthusiasm. An overly *zealous* person is a *zealot*.

cards.definition: to cut short
cards.example: The family decided to *abbreviate* their vacation when a hurricane threatened the island.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: the power to do something; skill or competence in a field
cards.example: Her *ability* to play the piano is staggering; she can play the hardest pieces effortlessly.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to shorten
cards.example: The novel was *abridged* so the students could read it in class.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to escape
cards.example: The thief *absconded* with the jewels.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: not in a certain place at a given time
cards.example: The student was *absent* from class.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: to take in or draw up
cards.example: We used a sponge to *absorb* most of the liquid that was spilled.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: difficult to understand
cards.example: Young children have a difficult time understanding *abstract* concepts such as time and space.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: possessing a lot of something; often more than is needed
cards.example: The food at Thanksgiving dinner was *abundant*; we spent the next two weeks eating leftovers.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to emphasize
cards.example: The vase used to *accent* the room brings out the colors in the rug.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to receive with pleasure; to agree
cards.example: The athlete was proud to *accept* the Olympic gold medal.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to be able to reach, approach, or enter; gain admission to
cards.example: I need the secret password to *access* my bank account.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: easy to approach or enter
cards.example: The presidential palace was *accessible* only to friends and family.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: an event that occurs by chance
cards.example: The couple met at a coffee shop by *accident*; neither of them had planned to see the other that day.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: very skilled or successful at something
cards.example: Stephen King is an *accomplished* writer, with over forty books to his name.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: an official treaty
cards.example: The rival factions ended their war with a peace *accord*.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: as indicated or stated by
cards.example: *According* to legend, King Arthur led the defense of Britain against the Saxon invaders in the sixth century.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to gather or collect
cards.example: The geologist was hoping to *accumulate* more rock specimens on his trip out West.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: free from error or defect; consistent with a standard, rule, or model; precise; exact
cards.example: The data presented by the scientist was *accurate*.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to accomplish something
cards.example: The Trojans were eventually able to *achieve* victory over the Greeks after a long, tragic war.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a chemical substance that dissolves some metals
cards.example: The polluted rain was an *acid*.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: the state of doing something
cards.example: In a large city, there is so much *activity* that it is difficult to find peace and quiet.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to be truly in existence
cards.example: Contrary to popular opinion, the war *actually* helped the country’s economy.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: sharp; shrewd; discerning
cards.example: The hound dog has an *acute* sense of smell.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to change according to conditions or requirements
cards.example: It will be difficult for the polar bear to *adapt* to the changing climate.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a change or alteration developed in response to one’s environment
cards.example: The cactus has developed an *adaptation* that allows it to survive without water for months at a time.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: more than what is necessary
cards.example: The house featured an *additional* bedroom that could be used as a guest room or an office.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to speak to someone directly in a formal way
cards.example: The president’s speech was an *address* to Congress.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: very skilled at something
cards.example: The Harlem Globetrotters are *adept* basketball players.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: enough for a required purpose
cards.example: She makes an *adequate* amount of money, but she still can’t afford to go on fancy vacations.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to stick to a surface; to follow the practices of; to believe in
cards.example:
The student put glue on the back of the paper so it would *adhere* to the poster.
The men *adhered* to the Muslim faith.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: located next to something; beside
cards.example: Our house is *adjacent* to the corner store.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: ahead of others in progress or sophistication
cards.example: Only the most *advanced* physics students can truly understand the Fermi Paradox.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: circumstances or traits that lead to success or a desirable outcome
cards.example: One of the many *advantages* of living in the country is that the air is cleaner.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: words offered as a guide to action
cards.example: I followed the doctor’s *advice* to stay at home and rest.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to recommend as a course of action
cards.example: I *advise* all my students to study a lot before exams.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: someone who supports a cause
cards.example: Elie Wiesel was a tireless *advocate* for peace.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: related to visual beauty
cards.example: His expert use of color and shadow made the painting an *aesthetic* success.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to produce a change in; to move the emotions of someone
cards.example: I hope your illness does not *affect* your ability to work.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: confrontational; assertive
cards.example: The bully was very *aggressive*; he picked fights daily.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: to share the same views or feelings
cards.example: I hope we can *agree* on a good time for us to meet.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to set aside a resource for a particular aim
cards.example: The company decided to *allocate* a portion of its profits to charity.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a loud and public disagreement or fight
cards.example: After the car accident, the drivers got upset and had an *altercation*.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: another choice
cards.example: We want an outdoor wedding, but we have an *alternative* location if it rains.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: generous and giving to others
cards.example: The minister was an *altruistic* man who gave the little money he earned back to the community.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: one who is new or unskilled at something
cards.example: Steve was an *amateur* at golf; he had only hit a ball with a club once.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: related to the surrounding environment
cards.example: The elevator music provided *ambient* noise while passengers rode to their floors.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: open to or having several possible meanings or interpretations; of doubtful or uncertain nature; difficult to comprehend, distinguish, or classify
cards.example: Sara gave an *ambiguous* answer to the lawyer’s question.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: having great determination for success
cards.example: The students were *ambitious*; they wanted to learn everything the school could teach them.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: undecided; having opposing feelings simultaneously
cards.example: The man was *ambivalent* about where to eat dinner; he couldn’t decide between chicken and fish.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a vehicle used to transport sick or injured people
cards.example: When the child broke his arm, the *ambulance* took him to the hospital.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: friendly; agreeable
cards.example: The golden retreiver was *amiable*; she excitedly greeted every person she saw.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: feeling loving, especially in a romantic sense
cards.example: On Valentine’s Day, Farhad was feeling *amorous* so he took his girlfriend to a romantic dinner.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a stadium used for concerts or performances
cards.example: While on vacation, the students visited an *amphitheater* in Rome called the Colosseum.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a breakdown of the components of a substance or phenomenon
cards.example: Our *analysis* of the object revealed that it was made of carbon.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: determine the elements or essential features of
cards.example: We must *analyze* your test to determine what you need to improve.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: something out of place in time or history
cards.example: The digital watch the general in the WWII drama wore on his wrist was an *anachronism*.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: very old; from the distant past
cards.example: The *ancient* temple of Angkor Wat is almost 900 years old.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a robot that looks or acts like a human
cards.example: The science-fiction film depicted an *android* that could serve as a robotic butler.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a historical record of events
cards.example: The historian referred to the *annals* of 10th-century Egyptians to write her paper.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to add or attach
cards.example: When the school ran out of classroom space in the main building, leaders built an *annex* behind it to house additional students.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: an unusual occurrence; an irregularity or deviation
cards.example: The Aurora Borealis is usually seen in high latitude regions like the Arctic, so it would be an *anomaly* if it were seen in New England.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a short speech designed to notify
cards.example: There was an *announcement* on the radio that school had been canceled because of bad weather.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: disturbed or bothered
cards.example: The sound of the car alarm downstairs *annoyed* the residents who were trying to sleep.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: occurring or returning once a year
cards.example: The parade is an *annual* affair.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: an unknown or withheld name
cards.example: The wealthy benefactor wished to remain *anonymous*; she didn’t want anyone to know her name.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: occurring before another event
cards.example: The heavy rain was an *antecedent* event to the flooding that occurred.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: the study of human society
cards.example: Those who had studied *anthropology* were excited to see the earliest known cookbook at the museum.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to expect or predict
cards.example: The dark clouds made him *anticipate* a storm.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: medicine used to counteract poison
cards.example: When the gardener was bit by the snake, the doctor gave him an *antidote* to prevent the poison from taking effect.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to be attractive or pleasing
cards.example: Eating snails is something that does not *appeal* to me.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: attractive
cards.example: With their soft fur and large eyes, puppies are *appealing* to almost everyone.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: the act of appearing; coming into sight
cards.example: The most exciting part of the film’s premiere was when the lead actress made her *appearance*.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to satisfy or relieve
cards.example: Congress was forced to compromise in order to *appease* the holdouts.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to put to use or assign
cards.example: The professor *applied* the chemistry theory to the equation and came up with the correct answer.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to value or be grateful for
cards.example: We often don’t *appreciate* the best things in life until they’ve been taken away from us.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to come near or closer to
cards.example: The celebrity was so intimidating, I was not sure how to *approach* him.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: suitable or fitting to the situation at hand
cards.example: A business suit is *appropriate* attire for the job interview.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: not exact, but close to accurate
cards.example: My plane will arrive at *approximately* 9 P.M.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: subject to individual will or discretion
cards.example: The boy who broke the lamp wasn’t the boy who was punished —it was frustratingly *arbitrary*.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: the typical example; an original that is copied
cards.example: Romeo and Juliet is a perfect *archetype* of the genre.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a person who designs structures
cards.example: Frank Lloyd Wright is a famous *architect* who designed buildings so that they would organically fit into their surroundings.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to disagree over
cards.example: Let’s try not to *argue* over who does the dishes tonight.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: an expression of creativity such as a painting or sculpture
cards.example: The Metropolitan Museum contains hundreds of paintings and sculptures that represent *art* across history.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: not occuring naturally
cards.example: The hockey player had several *artificial* teeth to replace the ones he had lost during the season.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: exhibiting visual taste or skill
cards.example: She was so *artistic* that even her fruit bowl was arranged in a beautiful manner.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to estimate officially the value of (property, income, etc.) as a basis for taxation; to impose a tax or other charge on; evaluate
cards.example: You must *assess* the effort you have put in to the task.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: something given to someone as a required task
cards.example: I was very busy this week, so I was unable to complete the homework *assignment*.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: help or support
cards.example: The old woman required *assistance* when getting in and out of cars.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to expect something to be true
cards.example: Given that you hate crowds, I *assumed* you wouldn’t want my extra ticket for the concert tonight.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: opinions which are taken for granted or presumed to be true
cards.example: I made some *assumptions* about Dana’s character without really knowing her.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: concentration of one’s thoughts or observations on a subject
cards.example: Make sure to pay *attention* in class, or you will have trouble with the homework
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: outlook on the world
cards.example: She had such an enthusiastic *attitude* that everyone enjoyed being around her.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to regard as resulting from a specified cause; consider as caused by something indicated (usually followed by to)
cards.example: Molly *attributed* her frustration to her lack of sleep.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to sell or offer to the highest bidder
cards.example: When the recluse died, his vast art collection was *auctioned* to raise money for community.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to make something greater
cards.example: The photographer wanted to *augment* her income by shooting weddings on the weekends.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: the power to determine, adjudicate, or otherwise settle issues or disputes; jurisdiction; the right to control, command, or determine
cards.example: The pastor had the *authority* to marry the couple.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a machine that works by itself
cards.example: The *automatic* dishwasher cleans the dishes without any work from the chef.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: independent or self-governing
cards.example: After years of being under Soviet rule, Lithuania finally became an *autonomous* nation in 1900.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: freedom from external control
cards.example: The Mohegan tribe has full *autonomy* on its own reservation.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.pron: uh vey luh BIL i tee
cards.definition: the quality of being around when needed
cards.example: The popular hotel is in such demand that it has limited *availability.*
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: able to be used, obtained, or accessed
cards.example: The shoes I wanted to order from the store are, unfortunately, no longer *available*.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: possessing knowledge
cards.example: Soldiers need to be *aware* of potential danger at all times, even when they least expect it.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a person’s education, knowledge, and cultural upbringing
cards.example: Her *background* in Romance languages was helpful in her trip through Europe.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: of prime importance; most necessary
cards.example: *Basic* human rights include the rights to free speech and property.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: to act as a friend; provide support
cards.example: Justin Timberlake *befriended* Jimmy Fallon at a chance meeting backstage in 2002; they have been close friends since that day.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: to have jealousy; envy
cards.example: Amy *begrudged* Jo’s book so much that she destroyed it in a fit of jealousy.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: the way in which one acts or conducts oneself; the manner in which something operates
cards.example: The child’s rude *behavior* irritated the guests.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: tardy, late, behind schedule
cards.example: When Jahnavi forgot her mom’s birthday, she sent a *belated* birthday gift one week later.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: things which are believed; convictions
cards.example: Many *beliefs*, such as the idea that the world is flat, turn out to be wrong.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: make someone or something feel unimportant; disparage
cards.example: My guidance counselor *belittled* my high school record by telling me that not everybody belongs in college.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: aggressive or threatening
cards.example: The mean bully was *belligerent*.
cards.notes: Negative connotation.

cards.definition: one who receives a benefit
cards.example: If your next-door neighbor rewrites his life insurance policy so that you will receive all his millions when he dies, then you become the *beneficiary* of the policy.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: a positive result or outcome
cards.example: One *benefit* of exercise is that you will have more energy throughout the day.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: an expression of kindness; a blessing
cards.example: In certain church services, a *benediction* is a particular kind of blessing.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: having kind wishes toward others
cards.example: The United Way, like any charity, is a *benevolent* organization.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: kind and gentle
cards.example: Charlie was worried that he had cancer, but the lump on his leg turned out to be *benign*.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: relating to or affecting two sides
cards.example: The two countries held a *bilateral* meeting in a neutral location.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: someone who speaks two languages fluently
cards.example: The *bilingual* teacher could speak fluently to her students in both English and Spanish.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: involving the agreement between two parties
cards.example: The agreement between Republicans and Democrats was *bipartisan*.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: the quality or state of being brief in duration
cards.example: The reader of this book may be grateful for the *brevity* of this example.
cards.notes: Positive connotation.

cards.definition: lasting or taking a short time; of short duration; using few words; concise
cards.example: We had a *brief* conversation on the way out the door.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: a large range or scope; not narrow
cards.example: The conference featured a *broad* range of topics, including everything from astrology to exercise.
cards.notes: Neutral connotation.

cards.definition: the physical grounds of an academic institution
